newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mediator is hopeful despite rebel defiance.
newsitem.headline: Peru mediator is hopeful despite rebel defiance.

text.p: A mediator in Peru's hostage crisis said he was hopeful the 41-day siege will be resolved peacefully despite the refusal of Marxist guerrillas to free their captives until the government meets their demands.
"There is a small light on the horizon," Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani said on Sunday outside the Japanese ambassador's residence where the rebels are holding 72 VIP hostages.

Cipriani, a friend of President Alberto Fujimori who has been accepted by both sides as a mediator, accompanied the head of Peru's Roman Catholic Church, Cardinal Augusto Vargas, on a half-hour visit to the hostages.

Emerging from the residence, the cardinal called for divine intervention to produce a breakthrough. "Men sometimes do not find a solution...now we need God to intervene," Vargas told reporters as Lima's church bells chimed.
The Tupac Amaru guerrillas freed an ailing police commander from the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence early on Sunday so that he could receive medical treatment.
But the rebels said they would not surrender in a daily megaphone broadcast that includes their revolutionary hymn.
"We've been here for 40 days and we are going to continue resisting," one guerrilla shouted from inside the house.
Gen. Jose Rivas Rodriguez, a deputy chief in the Peruvian national police, was wheeled out of the residence on a stretcher and rushed to a nearby police hospital.
The Red Cross said the other hostages were in good health. "The situation is calm. Given the circumstances, I think they are all well," Red Cross official Ruben Ortega said.
Rodriguez's release followed several days of tense posturing, with rebels firing warning shots into the air in response to what they called provocative movements by police.

In a war of nerves between police and guerrillas, two special forces officers signalled on Sunday to a female rebel at a window to leave the house and join them on the street. In reply, she gestured to the police to join her inside.

Police have thrown stones and garbage into the grounds, flown helicopters overhead and moved in armoured vehicles and men with high-powered rifles and night-vision equipment. A helicopter returned on Sunday, but kept further away.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is among the captives, has said the police manoeuvres were not a buildup to an assault and insisted he was seeking a negotiated end to the crisis.
But talks remain deadlocked with the rebels sticking to their main demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades and the government refusing to even discuss it.
Some 15 rebels took more than 500 hostages on Dec. 17 when they stormed a cocktail party at the diplomatic residence, but have freed most in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped house include two Peruvian ministers, congressmen, judges, police and army chiefs, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
